title: Thermal projection was 2 to 3 percent of squared family change across 1 to 12 years at selected English river sites
abstract: We tested whether weak annual thermal response meant little recorded community change or a response that increased over longer intervals. We used 3,715 autumn samples from 217 English river sites, trained composition directions on 1991-2000 records at other sites, and tested exact intervals within 2001-2017. Mean Hellinger distance rose from 0.712 at one year to 0.814 at 12 years. Only 1.78-2.87 percent of squared change lay along the early thermal direction, compared with 11.84 percent of squared differences between later sites sampled in the same year and month. The thermal slope had no steady rise over 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12 years. The 12-year minus one-year slope was -0.017, with a site-bootstrap range of -0.173 to 0.138. BOD and ammonia point slopes rose with interval, but calendar-year uncertainty limits this contrast. Habitat adjustment reduced the spatial thermal benchmark and made precise residual transfer claims unsafe. Twelve short-interval pairs at eight sites also had large distances; recorded change cannot be read as biological replacement alone. This study separates total recorded change from its direction. It does not identify demographic delay, causal thermal effects or a national warming response. Family records, air-temperature proxies, sample selection and incomplete observation-error information limit the result. Code, aggregate outputs, input hashes and external-data instructions are included.
